summary: Social coverage carried the heaviest negative weight this week: 24 of 65 social readings (37%) were negative, against 17% for political and 14% for economic. The social negatives came mostly from crime, safety and accident stories rather than politics. Two murder investigations drew sustained attention: in Karachi, a judicial commission called the police inquiry into businessman Mir Raza Ali's killing an "epic failure", prompting the Sindh government to bring intelligence and Rangers officials into a new joint investigation team, while in Rawalpindi the family of media executive Hina Javed wrote to the Punjab chief minister asking for a judicial probe, saying they distrust the police inquiry. Harassment cases in Lahore and Karachi, a child exploitation case reported by the NCCIA, a bus crash in Hafizabad that killed five, an oxygen cylinder blast at a Tharparkar health centre that killed eight, and Lahore topping a global pollution ranking added to the tally. Only five social readings were positive, among them a cricket selection story and the PM Chromebook scheme.

The week's dominant storyline, and the thread behind seven of its eleven flagged articles, was the deepening standoff between PTI and the state, centred on Khyber Pakhtunkhwa under governor's rule. Governor Faisal Karim Kundi said Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and the assembly speaker were under house arrest and "in safe hands", and suggested the October 11 emergency could last beyond six months; their relatives petitioned the Peshawar High Court. Days later an anti-terrorism court issued arrest warrants for Afridi and four other PTI leaders in the May 2023 Radio Pakistan attack case, evidence PTI disputes. Inside the party, a seven-hour parliamentary meeting saw most lawmakers argue against further talks with the establishment, according to Dawn and Business Recorder, while the prime minister's adviser Rana Sanaullah warned that parties not backing the fight against terrorism would be sidelined. The week closed with Lahore High Court judge Mohsin Akhtar Kayani resigning, citing his health and his view that the 26th and 27th amendments have weakened high court independence. Political negatives peaked on October 29, when four of eleven stories read negative.

Political lean stayed largely balanced despite this charged coverage: 60 of 65 articles read balanced, five pro-government and none pro-opposition. The pro-government readings were tied to sourcing, not to any position Miqyas takes: they appeared where a story relied on one side's account with no reply, such as Sanaullah's remarks and the information ministry's rejection of the Afghan Taliban's version of the Angoor Adda clash. That border incident shows the limits of the reporting clearly. Local officials said a civilian was killed and five family members wounded by fire from the Afghan side, and Pakistani security sources said several Afghan posts were destroyed in response; Islamabad called Kabul's account "fabricated" and alleged Indian involvement, and none of those claims were independently verified. AI confidence reflected this: 37 articles were rated medium against 26 high, October 26 had ten medium ratings among twelve stories, and the only two low ratings went to reports of militant commanders killed in Balochistan that rested on unnamed sources. Several of the most consequential political items, including the Kundi interview, the arrest warrants and the hospitalisation of Imran Khan's sister Noreen Niazi in custody, came through just one source each.

Economic coverage was the calmest category, with 83% neutral readings, but its nine negatives clustered toward the week's end: a sharply wider regional trade deficit, higher customs values on imported stationery raw materials, a scrapped vaccine tender, and a fuel price rise that brought diesel close to Rs400 a litre. The reopening of the Gabd border crossing with Iran and a government move toward a new umbrella privatisation entity supplied the only two positive economic readings. None of these economic stories were flagged for review, which suggests the week's sensitive material sat almost entirely in politics and security.

notableStories.headline: Justice Kayani resigns, citing growing control over the judiciary
notableStories.context: A sitting Lahore High Court judge stepped down citing his health and his view that the 26th and 27th amendments have eroded high court independence, a rare public signal of strain between the courts and the executive.

notableStories.headline: KP Governor Kundi says Sohail Afridi, assembly speaker 'in safe hands' after house arrest
notableStories.context: The governor confirmed that Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's elected chief minister and assembly speaker were being held under house arrest and suggested governor's rule could run beyond six months.

notableStories.headline: PTI asked to look inward; warned against further talks
notableStories.context: Most PTI lawmakers in a seven-hour meeting argued against more talks with the establishment and criticised the leadership after the failed long march and the loss of the KP government, exposing a split inside the main opposition party.

notableStories.headline: Pakistan strikes Afghan Taliban posts after cross-border attack
notableStories.context: Local officials said fire from the Afghan side killed a civilian and wounded five family members at Angoor Adda, and security sources said Pakistani forces struck Afghan Taliban posts in response, renewing hostilities on a key border trade route.

notableStories.headline: ISI, IB officials included in JIT formed to probe Mir Raza murder
notableStories.context: After a judicial commission called the police inquiry into a Karachi businessman's killing an "epic failure", Sindh brought intelligence and Rangers officials into a new investigation and ordered a separate probe into possible cover-up.
